                                         Figure 1. From unlabeled 3D assets and language instruction, L AYOUT VLM generates scene layouts that are physically plausible and
                                         semantically coherent—two criteria that existing methods often struggle to meet. Our approach addresses this by using a VLM to generate a
                                         scene layout representation that defines both an initial layout and spatial relations between assets for differentiable optimization.

  Type            Notation                             Explanation
  Positional      Ldistance (pi , pj , dmin , dmax )   The distance between the two assets should fall within the range [dmin , dmax ] .
  Positional      Lon_top_of (pi , pj , bi , bj )      Position one asset on top of another.
  Rotational      Lalign_with (pi , pj , ϕ)            Align two assets at a specified angle ϕ.
  Rotational      Lpoint_towards (pi , pj , ϕ)         Orient one asset to face another with a offset angle ϕ.
  Mix             Lagainst_wall (pi , wj , bi )        Place an asset again wall wj .

Table 1. Spatial Relation Definition. We define five spatial relations that determine how objects are placed relative to each other and within
the room. Each constraint is associated with a differentiable cost function based on the object poses, which can be used for optimization.
Our spatial relations related to rotation do not require a fixed reference frame and instead are based on relative poses between objects.

object poses and spatial relations, combining them within                   representation [6–9]. However, these generated scenes lack
a differentiable optimization framework to enable robust                    separable, manipulable objects and surfaces, rendering them

                                                                        2
                                                                            2.2. Vision-Language Models for 3D Reasoning
                                                                            Recent works have explored the spatial reasoning capabili-
                                                                            ties of vision-language models (VLMs). Some studies have
                                                                            trained 3D visual encoders on representations like point
                                                                            clouds and meshes to improve tasks such as 3D scene under-
                                                                            standing, question answering, navigation, and planning [15–
                                                                            21]. Other research has adapted 2D VLMs for spatial rea-
                                                                            soning by fine-tuning them on visual question-answering
                                                                            datasets involving metric and qualitative spatial relations
                                                                            grounded in 3D environments [22, 23]. A related direction is
                                                                            to reconstruct the 3D scene based on 2D images by training
                                                                            on large synthetic data [24]. However, these approaches
                                                                            primarily focus on perception tasks and do not extend to gen-
                                                                            erating 3D structures. In contrast, our work uses 2D VLMs
                                                                            for the task of 3D layout generation, utilizing techniques
                                                                            originally developed for visual reasoning—such as leverag-
                                                                            ing images of a scene from different viewing angles [25] and
                                                                            visual markers [26–28]—repurposed here for spatial plan-
                                                                            ning. We also investigate fine-tuning VLMs for 3D layout
                                                                            generation tasks and observe significant improvements in
                                                                            the performance of open-source models.


                                                                            3. Problem Formulation
                                                                            The problem of open-universe 3D layout generation is to
                                                                            arrange any assets within a 3D environment based on natural
                                                                            language instructions. Formally, given a layout criterion
                                                                            ℓlayout in natural language, a space defined by four walls
                                                                            oriented along the cardinal directions {w1 , . . . , w4 }, and a
                                                                            set of N 3D meshes {m1 , . . . , mN }, the goal is to create
                                                                            a 3D scene that faithfully represents the provided textual
                                                                            description. Following prior work [5, 14], we assume that
                                                                            the input 3D objects are upright and an off-the-shelf vision-
Figure 2. Example Scene Representation. Example of our scene                language model (VLM) (i.e., GPT-4o [29]) is employed to
representation for a bedroom. Our scene representation consists of          determine their front-facing orientations. The VLM also
numerical estimates of object poses and spatial relations correspond-       annotates each object with a short textual description si ,
ing to objective functions on these poses. Having the VLMs gener-           and the dimensions of its axis-aligned bounding box after
ate the initial estimates allows us to exploit the semantic knowledge       rotating to face the +x axis will be represented as bi ∈ R3 .
in the large models, and having spatial relations amenable to opti-         The target output of layout generation is each object’s pose
mization allows us to generate physically precise placements.               pi = (xi , yi , zi , θi ), including the object’s 3D position and
                                                                            rotation about the z-axis.

Evaluation. In our evaluation, we assess models’ abilities                   (Pos.) and Rotational Coherency (Rot.), measuring align-
in 1) open-vocabulary language instructions, 2) predicting                   ment with the input prompt. To evaluate semantic coherence
layouts for objects beyond predefined categories, and 3) gen-                across layouts without groundtruth, we use GPT-4o to score
erating accurate object placements within boundaries while                   layouts based on top-down and side-view renderings and
avoiding collisions. We create test cases across 11 room                     the language instructions, leveraging its effectiveness as a
types, with three rooms per type and up to 80 assets per                     human-aligned evaluator in text-to-3D generation [35]. We
room. Each test case includes human-verified, pre-processed                  also introduce the Physically-Grounded Semantic Alignment
3D assets sourced from Objaverse [34], language instruc-                     Score (PSA) to assess physical plausibility and semantic
tions generated by GPT-4, and a floor plan defining space                    alignment, assigning 0 if assets cannot be feasibly placed.
dimensions. All methods use the same pre-processed assets.                   PSA is calculated simply the GPT-4o rating weighted by

                                                                                                 6. Conclusion
                                                                                                 In this paper, we present L AYOUT VLM, a comprehensive
poses, without performing optimization. As shown in Ta-                                          framework for open-universe 3D layout generation, includ-
ble 5, the results confirm the effectiveness of our method’s                                     ing a novel scene layout representation that builds on two
design. Although w/o Visual still uses the same optimization                                     representations of layout from visually marked images: nu-
process, which improves physical feasibility, we observe                                         merical pose estimates and spatial relations. With the scene
a clear advantage in using a VLM. This likely stems from                                         layout representation combined with self-consistent decod-
the VLM’s ability to leverage rendered scenes and asset                                          ing, differentiable optimization, and visual prompting, we
views to enhance spatial planning (e.g., arranging groups                                        demonstrated significant improvements over existing LLM
of objects in distinct regions). The comparison with w/o                                         and constraint-based approaches. While L AYOUT VLM
Const. confirms that VLMs alone were insufficient; our                                           shows promise, it has limitations, including occasional fail-
scene representation—consisting of both numerical object                                         ures in generating valid layouts due to suboptimal VLM
poses and spatial relations-is essential for generating practi-                                  initializations. We hope our work paves the way for future
cal layouts. Finally, we observe that self-consistency takes                                     research to explore more complex scenes and address these
advantage of our scene representation to help ensure that                                        challenges, pushing the boundaries of 3D layout generation
placements met both physical and semantic requirements.                                          with improved semantic and physical reasoning.
We also analyze the effects of two key components in our
proposed scene layout representation. The results indicate
that spatial constraints are crucial for ensuring physical                                       Acknowledgments. This work is in part supported by
validity, particularly in preventing object overlap, while a                                     Google, Analog Devices, the Stanford Center for Inte-
good numerical initialization contributes to better semantic                                     grated Facility Engineering (CIFE), the Stanford Institute for
scores.                                                                                          Human-Centered AI (HAI), NSF CCRI #2120095, AFOSR
                                                                                                 YIP FA9550-23-1-0127, ONR N00014-23-1-2355, and ONR
5.5. Finetuning LayoutVLM                                                                        YIP N00014-24-1-2117.

In this experiment, we investigate whether fine-tuning pre-
trained VLMs with our scene layout representation improves
physical feasibility and semantic coherence. Specifically, we
compare this approach with fine-tuning VLMs to directly
predict numerical poses. Since the 3D-Front training data
consist of typical household room types, we evaluated the
fine-tuned models on test cases within the residential cate-
gory (i.e., bedroom, living room, and dining room). As these
test cases include unseen 3D assets from Objaverse and even
new object categories, this experiment also assessed gen-
eralization capability. We extract the ground-truth layouts
from 3D scenes by selecting defined spatial relations higher
than predetermined thresholds. The language instructions
are generated based on the type of rooms annotated in the
3D scene dataset. We finetune the open-sourced LLaVA-
NeXT-Interleave [33] model via LoRA and GPT4-o via the
publicly available finetuning API.

scene representation is more effective than using direct nu-

      100: Excellent: The layout of the scene (i.e.
           relative position and pose of objects in
           the scene) align very well with the
           criteria.
      80: Good: The layout of the scene mostly align
           with the criteria (only ~10% assets do not

           do not).

           criteria.

C. More Qualitative Comparison
In Figure 7, we present more qualitative examples of layouts
generated by L AYOUT VLM and baseline methods. L AY-
OUT VLM consistently outperforms baseline methods across
all room types in terms of both physcial plausibility and
semantic coherency. In the Living Room example, L AY-
OUT VLM excels in identifying semantic asset group by
clustering sofa and table together. By leveraging spatial rea-
soning from VLMs, we are able to stack assets toegther, as
shown in the Deli example.
